---
title: "Introduction"
---


Characterized by progressive cognitive decline that significantly impairs daily functioning and independence, dementia imposes a heavy burden on individuals, families, and healthcare systems [@RN31]. Substantial ongoing research has advanced the identification of therapeutic targets and the clinical evaluation of candidate small-molecule and biologic agents [@RN3; @RN2]. Given the complexity of dementia, including its slow progression, there is a critical need for early markers of current and prospective underlying disease change and for risk projection [@RN35; @RN93].

Epigenetic modifications such as DNA methylation and histone modification reflect the complex biological processes that regulate gene expression in response to current and prospective changes in the internal and external environment, including disease status [@RN20; @RN101]. Epigenetic markers are therefore well suited to studying the distinct signatures associated with transitions between stages of dementia, potentially serving as a mechanistic link between risk factors and dementia pathogenesis. Epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) of autopsied brain tissue have shown extensive methylation alterations associated with dementia pathology relative to controls [@RN34; @RN33]. However, autopsy findings are limited by their inherently cross-sectional nature and by their capture of tissue at the end stage of disease, so they cannot establish whether methylation differences precede the pathology or arise as a consequence of it [@RN26]. Blood-based methylation patterns are an accessible alternative that can reflect dynamic modulation of the biological processes driving dementia stages [@RN37]. In cross-sectional studies, EWAS of dementia have identified blood-based differentially methylated positions (DMPs) that distinguish among those with clinical diagnoses of Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and cognitively unimpaired groups [@RN38]. However, prior studies have not captured the proposed dementia continuum [@RN102], as they have restricted participants to those with specific traits, have been based on small sample sizes [@RN38; @RN42; @RN36] or a simplified dichotomous classification of disease status [@RN43; @RN42; @RN36; @RN40], or have had no [@RN38] or limited [@RN43; @RN42] longitudinal follow-up. Additionally, interpretation of findings is hampered by study-design differences, since cross-sectional and longitudinal designs can yield discrepant estimates of age-related change [@RN103], which impedes cross-stage and cross-study comparisons.

To identify broader epigenetic patterns within the dementia spectrum, prospective studies in the general population with a wide range of cognitive impairment are needed to address these gaps — including characterizing changes in methylation across more finely delineated dementia stages within the same population.

By leveraging detailed clinical phenotyping and extended follow-up in the Age, Gene/Environment Susceptibility-Reykjavik Study (AGES-Reykjavik) [@RN1], we aimed to examine whether baseline blood-based epigenetic patterns associate with prospective transitions into different stages of clinically defined dementia.
